title: Pyxis Health - Inference Readiness Audit (latency & throughput)
topics: hosted vs dedicated vs private deployment tradeoffs
cost vs latency tradeoffs and autoscaling
summary: Initial discovery with Pyxis Health on production readiness for inference. Customer runs a clinical-chat assistant with bursts during morning triage. They target p95 <= 350ms for 512-token completions, want 150 concurrent streams with graceful fallbacks. Investigated hosted vs dedicated vs private (VPC). Action items: share benchmark template, run 1-hour token/sec test on hosted, follow-up technical deep dive with internal infra team.

Pyxis to provide a sample prompt set and expected token lengths
Schedule SE-led deep dive to validate KV cache behavior with Pyxis infra (next week)
Run 1-hour hosted token/sec soak test (Redwood) and share results

Maya Chen: Configure and run 1-hour hosted token/sec test, deliver results and notes by 2026-11-22

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-18 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Samir (Redwood AE), Maya (Redwood SE), Jordan (CTO, Pyxis), Priya (Head of ML), Ethan (SRE)

Auto-summary (auto): quick discovery, p95 targets, concurrency and streaming verification requested

[00:00] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Samir from Redwood, this is Maya our systems SE. How are we doing, Jordan?
[00:14] Jordan: Good, thanks. Busy morning triage today so appreciate the time.
[00:20] Samir: Absolutely. Quick agenda — we want to understand your latency and throughput goals, your typical workload (tokens per request, streaming vs batch), and which deployment mode you're leaning toward — hosted, dedicated, or private VPC.
[00:34] Priya: Yeah, we'll start with the p95 goals. Right now our internal SLA is P ninety-five for end-to-end response at 400 to 500 ms for a 512-token response, but we're trying to push that lower. Ideally <= 350ms p95 including network.
[00:50] Maya: OK that helps. Is that for streaming responses or full completion latency?
[00:55] Priya: Mostly streaming, users see the first tokens right away, but we need the whole completion to be quick because some clients re-render based on full output.
[01:08] Ethan: And we typically have morning bursts — about 15 minute spikes — where concurrency jumps. Baseline concurrency is 40, spiking to ~150 concurrent live streams for up to 20 minutes.
[01:23] Samir: Good, that's concrete. A few clarifying Qs: what's your average prompt + expected generation length in tokens? Also, are you okay with partial fallbacks (e.g., degrade to a smaller variant) if latency targets are at risk?
[01:36] Jordan: Average prompt ~120 tokens, generation about 400 tokens, so 520 total. Priya: We can tune prompt size but those are realistic. Regarding fallbacks, we can tolerate a degrade to a smaller model with QA gating, but we'd like the platform to surface when that happens.
[01:55] Maya: Redwood can do policy-based routing and automatic fallback to compatible model variants. We also have KV cache/prefix caching which reduces token work on repeated prompts. One note: KV cache behavior is sensitive to session affinity and the backing cache TTL.
[02:10] Priya: Quick Q — some vendors call it K V cash in transcripts, so wanted to confirm — this cache persists across sessions?
[02:18] Maya: The KV cache is per session/route by default; you can configure cross-session caching for deterministic prompts but that has privacy implications. For healthcare data you'd want strict TTL and encryption.
[02:31] Ethan: On privacy, we need SOC2 and strong KMS integration. Also audit logs for all token-level calls.
[02:40] Samir: We can provide SOC 2 Type II docs and KMS/HSM integrations; audit log retention is configurable. We'll attach the security pack.
[02:49] Jordan: Great. Another practical constraint — our infra sits in a VPC with strict egress controls. If we go private deployment we need a managed control plane but no outbound to public internet from inference nodes.
[03:03] Maya: That's a common pattern. Our Private (VPC) deployment supports a customer-managed network and optionally an air-gapped package for on-prem. For your case we can do a private cluster with a control plane over a peered management VPC or on-prem bridge.
[03:19] Priya: Performance difference between hosted and dedicated — any numbers for p95 on a 40ms GPU for a 7B-ish model vs quantized variants?
[03:30] Maya: Rough ballpark: for a 7B open model, Hosted with our optimized runtime and continuous batching, we see p95s in the low hundreds of ms for 512-token streams on a single inference instance under moderate concurrency. Dedicated gives more predictable tail latency because you get reserved capacity and avoid noisy neighbors. Quantization helps per-token speed but may slightly affect quality; we typically recommend running evals to measure quality drop vs latency gain.
[03:57] Jordan: Do you have an example token/sec number we can use for planning?
[04:02] Maya: Sure. For streaming generation we quote tokens/sec per GPU for a given model and sequence length. Example (very approximate): 7B fp16: 1200-1800 tokens/sec sustained; 7B 4-bit quant: 1600-2300 tokens/sec. But these vary by token length and batch packing. Also real world user behaviour (short prompts, stop tokens) changes effective throughput.
[04:28] Priya: That difference is bigger than I expected for quantization. Any tradeoffs for streaming quality?
[04:34] Maya: Mostly minimal for many tasks but depends on temperature settings and model. We'll advise a small eval suite.
[04:42] Speaker 1: (mumbled) also curious about cold start effects on the p95 — is there warm pool options?
[04:48] Maya: Yes, we support warm pools and burst capacity. Dedicated clusters can maintain warm instances to avoid cold starts; hosted also supports a configurable warm pool for pinned routes.
[04:58] Jordan: On concurrency — we expect 150 concurrent live streams at peak. How do you recommend sizing? We currently see 60 RPS during peak but long lived streams.
[05:12] Samir: Streams are tricky because they tie up connections. Two knobs: concurrent stream count and per-stream token/sec. We typically model worst-case where each stream requires a certain sustained token/sec. For planning, we ask for a representative 10-minute window of user traffic — we'll run a tokenflow model to recommend GPUs and routing policy.
[05:30] Priya: We'll send a 10-minute trace.
[05:33] Ethan: Regarding networking, our VPC egress is NAT'd and we have a proxy that sometimes buffers responses — could that inflate p95?
[05:43] Maya: Yes, any intermediate proxy or client-side buffering can add tail. Best practice is to maintain a direct TLS connection to the inference endpoint or to use our streaming SDK which supports keepalive and low-latency chunking.
[05:56] Jordan: For the run-of-hosted test you mentioned, what does Redwood need from us?
[06:01] Samir: Ideally: (1) the prompt set, (2) expected token lengths and stop conditions, (3) desired p95 targets, (4) network location for test runner (we can run from our infra to model best-effort hosted latency or have you run from inside your VPC for private/dedicated approximation).
[06:17] Priya: We'll provide prompts and target p95 <= 350ms. We want baseline hosted numbers first.
[06:23] Maya: We'll run a 1-hour soak: step load to peak concurrency and measure p50/p95/p99 for both first-token latency and full completion. We'll export token/sec and per-route cost estimates into the benchmark sheet.
[06:36] Jordan: Cost sensitivity — our CFO asked about $/1000 tokens at the p95 target.
[06:42] Samir: We'll include an estimated unit economics sheet that shows $/k-token for hosted and for dedicated at different commit levels. Also show quantization impact.
[06:51] Speaker 2: (interrupt) are there recommended autoscale rules?
[06:54] Maya: For bursty streaming we recommend a mix: target-based autoscale for steady state and headroom-based for burst (pre-warm nodes when queue depth crosses threshold). Also use request throttling to protect SLOs.
[07:07] Priya: One more question — observability. We need token-level tracing and per-route p95 dashboards.
[07:14] Maya: Redwood Console exposes per-route token counts, latency histograms, trace links, and exportable logs. You can bind eval sets to routes so regression alerts are tied to specific prompt sets.
[07:25] Jordan: Awesome. If hosted numbers look good how long to move to dedicated?
[07:29] Samir: Dedicated provisioning lead time is typically a couple of weeks depending on capacity, shorter if you commit to reserved capacity. Private (VPC) takes longer because of networking and compliance gates.
[07:40] Ethan: For private, how do you handle keys? We must use our KMS and not let keys leave our control.
[07:45] Maya: We support customer KMS and HSM integration; keys can be stored in your KMS and Redwood uses envelope encryption. We'll document the flow.
[07:55] Priya: Let's talk benchmark specifics — what stats will you capture in the sheet?
[07:59] Maya: We'll capture p50/p90/p95/p99 for first byte and full completion, tokens/sec, sustained throughput, tail-latency contributors, CPU/GPU utilization, and cost/time. We'll also note model version, quantization, batch settings, and whether KV cache was used.
[08:17] Samir: We'll include a sample load script in the repo so you can re-run tests from your infra for private path comparators. Link will be in the spreadsheet.
[08:26] Jordan: Great. One edge-case — we have regulatory windows where throughput must be lower (e.g., additional de-identification step). That adds ~30-80ms per request. Can Redwood pipeline that step without adding more tail?
[08:39] Maya: We can run de-id as a preprocessor on a separate service or inline as a synchronous step. Inline adds to end-to-end latency; preprocessor shifts load but may be better for p95 guarantees. We can model both in the benchmark.
[08:52] Priya: Sounds good.
[08:55] Samir: Quick recap and owners — Samir will send benchmark spreadsheet and load script. Maya will run hosted 1-hour soak and share results. Pyxis (Jordan/Priya/Ethan) will share prompts and network diagram. We'll reconvene next week for a deeper SE-led session.
[09:13] Jordan: Works for us. Thanks.
[09:17] Priya: Thanks.
[09:19] Ethan: Thanks, bye.
[09:22] Samir: Bye.

Notes on transcript: occasional mis-transcriptions (K V cash, P ninety-five readout), speaker labels generic at times. Shared artifacts: benchmark spreadsheet (https://redwood.example/benchmarks/pyxis-2026), security pack (https://redwood.example/security/soc2), sample load repo (https://github.com/redwood-inference/bench-loads/tree/pyxis)

End of transcript.
